title: Tokenized dtype routing and attention shape adapter
creator: Samira Patel
description:
Problem: Our serving runtime pays a per-request penalty converting tensors between storage dtypes (INT8/FP8/FP16) and compute dtype during attention when the kernel chosen is incompatible with the request's token shapes or per-head sparsity pattern. This manifests as: extra memcpy/convert time, increased memory traffic on hot paths, and occasional backpressure that elevates p99 latency for mid-length requests (64-512 tokens) on mixed workloads.

Goal: Implement a token-aware dtype routing layer + an attention shape adapter that maps incoming requests to the optimal kernel flavor with minimal runtime overhead. Instead of globally choosing an INT8 or FP8 path by model, route at request (and where safe, per-token-window) granularity based on token sequence shape, head occupancy statistics, and recent KV cache dtype. The attention shape adapter will normalize layout mismatches (head grouping, sequence chunking) with light-weight view/stride transforms so we can reuse fast quantized kernels more often.

Scope and success metrics:
- Implement routing + adapter for decoder-attention and cross-attention kernels only (no FFN changes in this ticket).
- Microbench target: reduce median token generation latency by >= 10% for mixed-dtype traces; reduce conversion overhead (measured as memcpy + dtype-convert) by >= 25%.
- Cost target: reduce token compute time (measured on p3/rt-gpu) by >= 7% on sample SLO workloads.
- Safety: no change to model outputs or numeric stability beyond floating-point rounding; must preserve deterministic output when a customer has deterministic inference enabled.

Approach:
1) Instrument token stream to collect lightweight features (sequence length, per-head activation sparsity estimate, cached KV dtype). These features live for the request lifespan and are updated in the request context (not global).
2) Build a small decision table (ordered rules, not a heavy ML model) that favors: exact-shape kernel match -> quantized fastpath; else adapter + quantized kernel if shape mapping cost < dtype-conversion cost; else fallback to mixed-precision kernel. Table tuned from offline benchmarks.
3) Implement attention shape adapter primitives: zero-copy stride reinterprets, head-grouping aggregator (for models with head counts not divisible by kernel pack size), and token-window stitcher to split long sequences into shapes friendly to tiled quantized kernels. All adapters should prefer views and pointer arithmetic; only fall back to memcpy when strictly required.
4) Scheduler integration: add a per-request small-cost hook in the pre-scheduling pipeline so the router's decision influences kernel selection when building batched jobs. Ensure that batching logic still coalesces compatible decisions and that incompatible choices split batches only when net cost improves.
5) Telemetry & fallback: emit routing decisions, adapter usage, decision latency, and per-request predicted vs actual savings. Provide a safety flag to force legacy behavior for canary cohorts.

Deliverables:
- Runtime change: routing + adapter + scheduler hook + unit tests.
- Benchmark harness: synthetic traces covering 1) short bursts (8-32 tokens), 2) mid-length (64-512), 3) long context stitching (1k+), and 4) real production trace sample.
- Design doc: confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Tokenized+Dtype+Routing+Design (link attached).
- Canary plan: 1% traffic for 48h -> 10% for 72h -> rollout. Rollback on p99 latency spike >10% over baseline or error rate increase >0.1%.

Trade-offs, open questions:
- Extra decision logic adds CPU cycles; need to validate that these do not erode gains on very short sequences. We will measure decision latency and add a fast-path no-op when shapes obviously match.
- Per-token-window routing demands careful reasoning with KV cache dtype; if the cached KV dtype differs from incoming request dtype we must prefer conversion vs adapter — we will codify an explicit threshold.
- Edge case: reproducibility/determinism for customers that pin seeds; must implement a deterministic routing table lookup path.

Risks:
- Increased complexity in batch coalescing may cause less effective GPU batching if not tuned.
- Head-grouping view transforms may expose alignment bugs on some weight layouts; plans include weight-layout checks and unit tests across existing layout permutations.

Rollout plan: dev -> internal perf cluster -> canary -> gradual rollout.
